Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/skills/dg-engineering-writing-style

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses the two `max()` paddings given under Responsive, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side, where backgrounds reach that edge while the gutter keeps text and controls clear. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's `env(safe-area-inset-*, 0px)` to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too), a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`, with the band above it painted by a fixed `body::before` (`content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10`) in its background, or in the page's where it starts lower.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#name` passes between the artifact's link and `location.hash`, never `#/path`, `#key=value`, a `pushState` path or a query string. The address bar on the artifact's own page and Share's Copy link follow the page's hash; beside a chat, in a project or in an app the bar may not. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending, route on the hash: name each in ASCII letters, digits and hyphens (never `settings`, `sidebar`, `customize`, `upgrade`, `downloads` or `comment-*`, which claude.ai reserves) and show the one in `location.hash`, or the start view if none, on load and on `hashchange`. Keep other state in the page, and keys, tokens or private values out of the hash: it shows in history and copied links.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside the `:root` padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets the `:root` padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

  ## Findings: MCP tool output-shape changes, tool rollout, and versioning
  
  ### 1. What the MCP spec says (current revision 2026-07-28)
  Source: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools and https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog
  
  - **outputSchema and structuredContent.** If a tool declares `outputSchema`, the server MUST return conforming `structuredContent`, and clients SHOULD validate it. The spec also says a tool SHOULD return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block "for backwards compatibility". The spec does not say what a client does when validation fails; that is left to the implementation.
  - **What actually happens on a mismatch.**
    - TS SDK server (`McpServer`): checks `structuredContent` against `outputSchema` before sending, so the call fails on our side (https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/servers/tools).
    - TS SDK client, v1.x `Client.callTool` (read in source): throws `McpError` with "Structured content does not match the tool's output schema", or throws if the schema exists but no `structuredContent` came back.
    - The client compiles validators from the last `tools/list`, so validation is only as fresh as that list (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/v1.x/src/client/index.ts). The Go SDK returns the same failure as error -32602 (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/issues/386).
    - **What this means for us:** `outputSchema` is a hard contract. A shape change that doesn't update the schema surfaces as a protocol error, not as slightly different data.
  - **No initialize step any more.** 2026-07-28 removed `initialize`. `serverInfo` now goes in each result's `_meta` (`io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`), clientInfo goes in each request, and there is a new `server/discover` RPC.
    - `serverInfo.version` is only for identification. Nothing in the protocol consumes it to negotiate tool versions.
    - The spec has **no per-tool versioning mechanism.** The only related guidance is the tool-name charset, whose examples include names like `DATA_EXPORT_v2`.
  - **Tool-list freshness.** `tools/list` results must now carry `ttlMs` and `cacheScope`. `notifications/tools/list_changed` is delivered over `subscriptions/listen` and immediately invalidates a cached list (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/utilities/caching). Annotations stay hints that clients must treat as untrusted.
  - **Why list_changed doesn't help us.** For an npx stdio server, tool definitions are fixed in the installed code. They only change when a new process starts on a new package version. list_changed would matter only if we generated tool definitions at runtime, for example from a server-fetched manifest.
  - **How clients cache tool lists:**
    - **Claude Code** (docs): re-fetches the tool list on list_changed in interactive mode, keeps the old list if the refresh fails, and `/mcp` Reconnect drops the cached list (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp). Several issue reports say list_changed is ignored, so behaviour likely depends on the version.
    - **Cursor:** forum reports say list_changed is ignored or regressed, and that a restart or an `mcp.json` edit is the workaround (https://forum.cursor.com/t/mcp-notifications-tools-list-changed-not-acted-on-mid-session/161459). Not officially documented.
    - **Codex and Claude Desktop:** I could not verify either. The only Codex item I found was a feature request for a refresh command (https://community.openai.com/t/mcp-server-refresh-for-codex-cli-please/1380449).
    - **Practical assumption:** tool definitions are frozen for the whole session.
  
  ### 2. Impact on the agent side
  Source: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
  
  - **Field names are a contract.** Skills, prompts, CLAUDE.md snippets, chained agents and user scripts reference names like `node.title` and IDs to pass to the next call. Renaming or removing a field breaks them silently. The agent improvises, and you get no error unless `outputSchema` validation catches it.
  - **Keep or rename the tool?**
    - If the meaning is the same and the change is additive, keep the name.
    - If the output contract breaks, prefer a new name (`get_node_v2`, or a better descriptive name) or an opt-in parameter such as `response_format`.
    - Swapping the shape under an unchanged name, with an unchanged description, is the worst case for agents and for cached tool lists.
  - **Article guidance that applies here:**
    - Return high-signal, natural-language fields, but keep the IDs needed to chain calls.
    - Offer a `concise`/`detailed` response format. This is a natural place for a second shape to live.
    - Use strict output models.
    - Write actionable error messages.
    - Re-run evals after any tool change.
  - **The `content` text matters too.** Many clients pass only `content` text to the model. If that short text summary changes, model behaviour can change even when `structuredContent` is identical.
  
  ### 3. Versioning patterns for clients you can't force-update
  - **Additive-only v1 and v2 alongside.** This is standard and fits our rule. A field change counts as breaking if it renames, retypes, removes, or changes nullability.
  - **Deprecation signals.** Use the `Deprecation` header (RFC 9745, structured-date value like `@1767225600`, plus a `Link rel="deprecation"` to docs) and the `Sunset` header (RFC 8594, HTTP-date): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594.
    - Our MCP must log these headers itself, because nobody else will see them.
    - Once sunset, return a JSON body. 410 is appropriate. Avoid 426: it formally requires an `Upgrade` protocol header.
  - **Minimum client version.** Have the MCP send `User-Agent: dg-mcp/<pkg version>` or `X-DG-MCP-Version`.
    - The website can then measure which versions still call each route, which is how you decide when to sunset.
    - It can also reject versions that are too old with a structured "upgrade required" body.
    - The MCP then turns that body into an `isError: true` tool result whose text says "restart your MCP client so npx fetches the latest version". The agent can relay that message. An opaque failure would not be relayable.
    - **We should ship this header and handling in the very next release.** Copies installed before it can never be identified or told to upgrade.
  - **Server-side indirection.** Keep a stable path per tool, a backend-for-frontend route the MCP owns, and change what's behind it.
  - **Adapter in the MCP.** Map the new upstream shape to the old tool output.
  - **Stripe-style date pinning.** Each account is pinned to the API version from its first request, and a `Stripe-Version` header can override it. Internally the server keeps a chain of "version change" transforms that rewrite current responses back to older shapes, so one implementation serves every version (https://stripe.com/blog/api-versioning). For us the equivalent is: the MCP sends a compile-time `API-Version`, and the route transforms the response down to it.
  
  ### 4. Work breakdown for `get_node`: internal route to `api/v1/nodes/[nodeId]`
  
  **Caveat that applies to every strategy.** Once a published npm build calls `api/v1/internal/nodes/[nodeId]`, that route is effectively public API. It has unknown callers, can't be force-updated, and is bound by the same additive-only rule. Either treat `internal` as "MCP-only public" from day one (version it, document it, add the version header and metrics), or don't ship it in a public build.
  
  **(A) Server-side: keep the MCP's route and change the implementation behind it (no MCP release)**
  - **Touched:** the internal route handler, which calls the same service or query as the public route and maps to the old response shape. Shared Zod response schema (unchanged). Route contract tests: snapshot of the old shape plus a parse against the old Zod schema.
  - **Old installed copies:** nothing changes, provided the response stays a superset of the old one.
  - **How long the old route lives:** indefinitely, or until version metrics show no callers. It becomes the stable façade.
  - **Effort:** S. This is the default whenever the new route's data is a superset of the old.
  
  **(B) MCP release that calls the new route and adapts it to the existing tool output (tool contract unchanged)**
  - **Touched:**
    - Tool handler: change the URL and add an adapter from the new shape to the old one.
    - Zod: parse the new response with the public schema, then emit the old output schema. `outputSchema` stays the same.
    - Unit tests: adapter fixtures from real responses of both routes, plus an assertion that the output validates against `outputSchema`.
    - Integration test against the public route.
    - Changelog and a semver minor or patch npm release. No agent-facing doc change.
  - **Old installed copies:** keep calling the internal route. Nothing breaks, but they stay pinned to it.
  - **How long the old route lives:** until metrics show old versions gone. This needs the version header from section 3. Without it, the window is "forever, or accept breakage". Add Deprecation and Sunset headers to the internal route.
  - **Effort:** M, mostly adapter, tests and the sunset tracking. Fields the old shape has but the public route lacks must be derived or nulled, which can turn this into an L.
  
  **(C) MCP release that exposes the new shape (tool output contract changes)**
  - **Touched:**
    - Tool handler, plus a new `outputSchema` generated from the public Zod schema.
    - Tool description and the `content` text summary.
    - Ideally a new tool name, or `get_node` with an opt-in format parameter, so old agents and skills aren't silently broken.
    - Updates to every skill, prompt and doc that references the old fields.
    - Evals re-run on agent flows.
    - Tests: schema conformance and description snapshot.
    - Major semver release with migration notes.
  - **Old installed copies:** keep calling the internal route with the old contract, so they're fine while it lives. New installs get the new contract. Users' skills written against old fields break on upgrade, and since `@latest` upgrades happen silently, they will break unannounced.
  - **How long the old route lives:** same as (B). Two tool contracts are now in circulation for an extended period.
  - **Effort:** L. The code change is moderate; most of the cost is documentation, skill updates and coordinating the communication.
  
  **Recommendation from this evidence:** add the client-version header and structured upgrade errors now. Prefer (A), and use (B) when you want to retire the internal route. Use (C) only under a new tool name.
  
  ### Not verified
  - Claude Desktop's and Codex's per-session tool caching and list_changed handling.
  - Whether Cursor's list_changed support is current.
  - Whether the TS SDK v2 client keeps the v1 throw-on-mismatch behaviour. I only read the v1.x source; the v2 server docs confirm server-side validation.

  ## How MCP server updates reach users (checked against docs and source as of 2026-11-20)
  
  **Bottom line:** With `npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest`, current npm checks the registry on every launch and installs a new version if one exists. The update takes effect only when the client restarts the stdio process: quit and reopen Claude Desktop, use `/mcp` → Reconnect (or restart) in Claude Code, or restart Codex. Nothing tells the user an update exists. If you need to detect stale clients, your server has to do it itself.
  
  ### 1. npx / uvx mechanics
  - **(a) How the update arrives.** I read the current npm source (`workspaces/libnpmexec/lib/index.js`, npm/cli `latest`). Every manifest lookup runs with `preferOnline: true`, so npm revalidates the package metadata with the registry on each launch.
    - **`pkg@latest` (a tag):** npx resolves the tag and compares the resolved tarball with the copy in `~/.npm/_npx/<hash>`. If they differ, it installs the new version. This is the same in the v9.9.3, v10.2.0, v10.9.0 and current source.
    - **Bare `pkg` (no version):** in the npx cache it is treated the same way (`npxByNameOnly`). But if the package is installed in the client's working-directory project or globally, npx runs that copy, which may be old. npx docs: "Package names provided without a specifier will be matched with whatever version exists in the local project." So `@latest` protects you from an old `npm i -g` copy; a bare name does not. https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx
    - **Exact pin (`pkg@1.2.3`):** never changes. Updating means editing the config.
    - **Ranges (`pkg@^1`):** older npm could keep a stale cached match. Fixed Feb 2025 (commit 8461186). https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/7838
    - **Old reports:** the many "npx serves a stale copy" threads mostly concern npm 6/7 or ranges. https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/1935
    - **Cache key:** the `_npx` folder is a hash of the spec string, so `pkg` and `pkg@latest` get separate cache folders.
  - **(b) What the user does:** restart the client. Nothing else.
  - **(c) Speed and reliability:** the next launch after you publish. Not verified:
    - What happens offline. My expectation is that npm fails or falls back to its HTTP cache; I did not test it.
    - How long the npm registry's CDN keeps serving the old package metadata after a publish. A related `npm pack` stale-metadata bug was fixed in March 2026 (https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/9045).
  - **Costs:** every launch makes a network call, which adds startup time. Codex's default `startup_timeout_sec` is 10 seconds.
  - **Risk:** `@latest` delivers breaking releases instantly and you cannot hold users back.
  - **(d) Non-technical users:** good. Nothing to do beyond a restart.
  - **uvx:** reuses the cached copy "unless a different version is requested". `pkg@latest` refreshes the cache. If the user ran `uv tool install`, that installed version wins unless `@latest` is given. So for uvx, use `@latest` explicitly. https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/tools/
  
  ### 2. When the update takes effect (all clients)
  The client starts the stdio process when it launches. A new version runs only after that process is restarted.
  - **Claude Desktop:** "completely quit Claude Desktop and restart it." https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers
  - **Claude Code:**
    - `/mcp` → **Reconnect** for one server.
    - `/mcp reconnect all` (needs v2.1.284 or later) retries all failed or unauthenticated servers, so I'm not sure it restarts a healthy one.
    - A `list_changed` notification refreshes tools only within the running process; it never swaps in a new binary.
    - `claude -p` runs pick up the new version on the next run. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
  - **Codex:** no reconnect command is documented. The desktop app has "Restart" and the IDE extension has "Restart extension".
    - Watch-out: `startup_readiness = "catalog"` lets a cached tool list satisfy startup while the server connects, so the tool list Codex shows can briefly be older than the running server. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli
  - **Cursor / VS Code:** not researched. Both have per-server restart controls in their MCP UI, but I did not confirm current details.
  
  ### 3. Claude Desktop extensions (.mcpb)
  - **(a) How the update arrives:**
    - Directory extensions "update automatically by default". Privately distributed `.mcpb` files must be "install[ed] manually". https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10949351
    - **Major change, current docs:** "Desktop extension listings in the directory are deprecated, and the directory no longer accepts MCPB submissions. To distribute a local MCP server through the directory, include it in a plugin." https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/mcpb.md
    - So a new `@discourse-graphs` `.mcpb` would be a manual download. Every update means downloading the new file and double-clicking it again.
  - **How updates are signalled:** not documented for privately distributed files. Assume users are never told.
  - **(d) Non-technical users:** installing is the easiest of all options (bundled Node, settings form generated from the manifest). Updating is the worst.
  
  ### 4. Plugins (the new directory route; Claude Code is documented)
  - **(a)** You bump `version` in `plugin.json`, or omit `version` so users track commits. Users get the new copy through background auto-update or by running `/plugin marketplace update` or `claude plugin update`.
  - **(b) Watch-out:** auto-update is **off by default for third-party marketplaces**, and `marketplace.json` has no field to turn it on. Each user toggles it in `/plugin` → Marketplaces, or an admin sets it in managed settings.
  - **(c) Watch-out:** if you keep the same `version` string, users never get new commits.
  - **Partial lever:** a plugin's MCP config could still point at `npx …@latest`, which avoids depending on plugin updates for the server code.
  - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/host-marketplace.md
  - Not verified: whether Anthropic's official directory marketplace auto-updates by default.
  
  ### 5. Registries and catalogs
  - **Official MCP Registry:**
    - Still "in preview". It holds metadata only: `server.json` points at the npm package. Every publish needs a new, unique version string, and published entries cannot be changed.
    - Docs say it is "not intended to be directly consumed by host applications". Aggregators are expected to sync roughly hourly.
    - I found **no client that auto-updates from it**. Publishing helps people discover the server; it does not deliver updates.
    - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/registry/about, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/registry/versioning
  - **Docker MCP Catalog / Toolkit:**
    - Docker builds and signs local servers in the `mcp/` namespace. Teams can "control which server versions" they use through custom catalogs.
    - New listings appear within about 24 hours of approval.
    - The docs don't cover how image updates reach users (tags, pull behaviour). Unverified. https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-catalog-and-toolkit/catalog/
  - **Smithery:**
    - Its hosted services, CLI and SDKs **shut down on 2026-10-31**. It is now only a non-proxied directory, run by Arcade.
    - Don't build on it. https://smithery.ai/future
  
  ### 6. Remote (Streamable HTTP) servers
  - **(a)** You deploy, and every user is on the new code immediately. Anthropic lists "Centralized updates pushed to all users" as a reason to choose remote over MCPB (mcpb.md, link above).
  - **What clients cache:**
    - The tool list, until a `list_changed` notification or a reconnect. Claude Code keeps the last list if a refresh fails.
    - Codex can start from a cached tool list (see §2).
  - **(b)** At most a reconnect.
  - **(d)** Best fit, but it means running a hosted service with OAuth, which conflicts with your local session-state design.
  
  ### 7. Git-checkout installs
  Updating means `git pull`, `pnpm install` if dependencies changed, then restart the client. Speed depends entirely on the user remembering to do it. Fine for contributors; not workable for non-technical users. (No source needed.)
  
  ### 8. What other servers do
  - **Playwright MCP:** every client snippet uses `npx @playwright/mcp@latest`. https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp
  - **Sentry:**
    - Its main offering is the remote `https://mcp.sentry.dev`.
    - Local use now goes through the Sentry CLI's `sentry mcp`.
    - `npx @sentry/mcp-server@latest` is labelled "Legacy". https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-mcp
  - **GitHub:**
    - Recommends the remote server first. The local server is a fallback for clients without remote support.
    - The local Docker image `ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server` is untagged in the examples, with no update guidance.
    - Renamed tools keep their old names "as aliases for backward compatibility".
    - https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server
  - **Figma:** not verified.
  - **Update warnings:** I found **no** popular server with a built-in "you're out of date" warning or minimum-version check. Not found, not proven absent.
    - If you want one, a self-built option: the server compares its own version with the npm registry at startup and puts a notice in its `instructions` or tool results.
  
  ### Recommendation for `@discourse-graphs/mcp`
  - Keep `npx -y …@latest`. Never tell users to `npm i -g`.
  - Restart the client is the only user step; document it per client.
  - Keep the session-state file format backward-compatible across versions, because users jump to new versions with no warning and you can't hold them back.
  - Add a server-side minimum-version check, so a user who is behind gets told.
  - An `.mcpb` makes installing easier but makes updating manual. A plugin needs the user to turn on auto-update. A remote server is the only option where updates reach every user with nothing on their side.
  
  ### Couldn't verify
  - npx behaviour offline.
  - How long the npm registry CDN serves old package metadata after a publish.
  - How Claude Desktop signals updates for extensions.
  - Default auto-update for the official Anthropic plugin directory.
  - Cursor / VS Code restart UX.
  - How Docker catalog image updates reach users.
  - Figma's approach.
</agent-message>

Contents
  1. 1How updates reach users
  2. 2Distribution options compared
  3. 3Switching a tool's endpoint
  4. 4Proposed spec edits
  5. 5Open items

ENG-25122026-11-20Research only · no code changed

How MCP updates reach users, and what an API endpoint switch costs

Input for the OpenSpec change headless-mcp-retrieval (Roam block igzkQFr4r), Decisions 1, 8 and 9.

Keep the local npx @latest MCP from the spec. Ship a version header and an "upgrade required" error in its first release.

With npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest, a new npm release reaches every user the next time their agent client restarts the MCP process. Nobody has to run a command. The gap is everything else: users aren't told an update exists, some never restart, and we can't see who is behind. Each of the three things to add first takes about a day. The MCP sends its version on every API call, the API can refuse versions that are too old with a message the agent can relay, and the session state file keeps a backward-compatible format. Once they ship, endpoint changes become server-side decisions instead of hopes about user behavior.

A remote (hosted HTTP) MCP is the only option where every user gets an update instantly. The spec rejected it on 2026-11-10 because of the hosted credential store it needs. Most of what it offers we already get: the MCP is a thin client, so retrieval fixes deploy with the website. The version header gets us most of the rest, which is knowing who is behind and being able to tell them, without hosting anything.

Small source toggles after claims hold where each one came from. You can read the brief straight through without opening them.

How does an MCP update propagate to users, especially for a local MCP?

What happens between npm publish and a user running the new code.
  • A local MCP updates when its process restarts. The agent client starts the stdio process when it launches and keeps it running. A newly published version runs only after that process restarts.
    sourceClaude Desktop: "completely quit Claude Desktop and restart it", modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers. Claude Code: /mcp → Reconnect, code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp. Codex: no reconnect command is documented; the app has Restart. Via research subagent.
  • @latest re-checks npm on every launch. npx looks up the tag's manifest with preferOnline: true. If the resolved version differs from its cached copy, it installs the new one. A restart is all the user has to do.
    sourceVerified myself on npm 10.9.8: libnpmexec/lib/index.js:27 (pacote.manifest(spec, {...flatOptions, preferOnline: true})) and :40 (tag specs skip the "anything in the tree matches" shortcut). The subagent reports the same logic in v9.9.3 through current.
  • A bare package name is weaker than @latest. Without a tag, npx runs a copy installed in the project or globally, even an old one. Exact pins never update. Setup docs should always say @latest and never npm i -g.
    sourcenpx docs: "Package names provided without a specifier will be matched with whatever version exists in the local project", docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx. The stale-cache bug for ranges was fixed in Feb 2025 (npm/cli#7838).
  • Nobody is told. No client shows "update available" for a local MCP. No popular server we checked warns users who are out of date. If we want to know or tell, the server has to do it itself.
    sourceSubagent survey of Playwright, Sentry and GitHub MCP servers. Absence of evidence, not proof of absence.
  • We can't hold users back either. @latest delivers a breaking release on the next restart. Users have no grace period, so the state file in ~/.discourse-graphs/mcp/ must stay readable by every future version.
  • Old versions linger. These users run old code indefinitely:
    • users who keep their client open for weeks;
    • users who pinned a version;
    • users whose npx resolves an old global install.
    So "every user updates" never happens. The API has to tolerate older versions until we can measure that they're gone.

The MCP spec's notifications/tools/list_changed doesn't help here. It refreshes the tool list inside a running process. It never swaps in new code, and a new npx version brings its tool definitions with it at startup.

sourceMCP spec, tools and caching pages (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools). Client support for list_changed is uneven: Claude Code documents it, and Cursor forum reports say it's ignored. Via subagent.

Distribution options compared

Six ways to ship the MCP to public users, by how updates arrive and who has to act.

TouchedRoute handler and a contract test against the old Zod schemaTool handler, adapter, fixtures from both routes, integration test, minor npm releaseTool handler, schema, description, docs, skills that use old fields, evals, major npm release
Old installed copiesunaffectedunaffectedstill call the old routeunaffectedstill call the old route; upgraded users' skills break silently
Old route livesIndefinitely, as a stable façadeUntil the version header shows no callersUntil the version header shows no callers
MCP release needednoyesminoryesmajor
EffortSa day or twoMabout a week; L if the public route lacks fields the old shape hadLmost of the cost is docs and communication
sourceJudgement. The S/M/L estimates come from the research subagent and me, inferred from the touched-file list, not measured. B grows to L when the old shape's fields must be derived or set to null.
  • Default to A. It works whenever the new route's data is a superset of the old route's. It also matches Decision 1, where fixes ship by deploying the website.
  • Use B to retire a route. It only works once the version header tells us when old callers are gone. Without the header, the old route lives forever, or we accept that it breaks for an unknown number of users.
  • Use C only under a new tool name, or behind an opt-in format parameter. Never swap the shape under an unchanged name and description.
  • Send deprecation signals the MCP can read. Put Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) headers on old routes. After the sunset, return a JSON error body. Only our MCP sees these headers, so it has to log them or turn them into a notice.

Proposed edits to the OpenSpec change

Small additions to headless-mcp-retrieval that make the above possible from v0.
  • Decision 8: add a version header. The MCP sends User-Agent: discourse-graphs-mcp/<version> on every call, and the API logs the version next to the request ID and operation. That log is how we decide when a route can be retired.
  • Decision 8: add an upgrade_required error code. Give it a safe message telling the user to restart their agent client. The MCP passes it through as a tool error, like other codes, so the agent can relay it. Use HTTP 410 or 422, not 426, because 426 requires an Upgrade header.
  • Decision 9: version the state file. Add a version field to ~/.discourse-graphs/mcp/<name>.json, and require each release to read every earlier format.
  • Task 5.4: add verification. Unit tests that the header is sent and that upgrade_required maps to a tool error.
  • Task 6.2: add a setup README line. Tell users to restart the client to update, and never to install the package globally.

None of these changes the four routes or tools. They are additive, and they're cheapest to add before the first public install exists.

Open items

What couldn't be settled, and what a wrong guess costs.
  • How long npm keeps serving old package metadata after a publish. Not tested. If it's slow, a fast-follow fix takes longer to reach users. The cost is low, because the API can patch around it.
  • What npx @latest does offline. Not tested. If it fails rather than falling back to the cached copy, the MCP won't start on a plane. The cost is low, because retrieval needs the network anyway.
  • Codex and Claude Desktop tool caching. We don't know whether they honor list_changed or for how long they cache tool lists. Codex can start from a cached tool list. If that list is stale, the agent may briefly see old tool definitions after an update. The cost is medium for option C and none for A or B.
  • Whether Anthropic's official plugin directory auto-updates by default. Unverified. It matters only if we choose the plugin route after v0.
  • Startup cost. @latest does a registry round trip on every launch, and Codex's default startup timeout is 10 seconds. Not measured. Check it during task 7.1.

Sources and method

How this was put together, and what was checked first-hand.
  • Spec context: openspec/changes/headless-mcp-retrieval/ (design.md Decisions 1, 8, 9; tasks.md groups 5 to 7; specs/discourse-mcp/spec.md), read locally on 2026-11-20.
  • Verified first-hand: npx tag resolution in npm 10.9.8 libnpmexec/lib/index.js:24-40.
  • Research subagents (two, with separate sources):
    • One covered distribution and update mechanics: npm and uv docs, Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Codex docs, MCPB, the MCP Registry, Docker, Smithery, and popular servers.
    • The other covered tool contracts and versioning: the MCP spec, the TypeScript SDK source, Anthropic's "Writing tools for agents", RFC 8594 and 9745, and Stripe's versioning post.
    Their claims are marked "via subagent" in the source toggles.

{"id":"ENG-2512","uuid":"4f734026-100d-42db-b914-44cdd18661cd","title":"Research how MCP server updates reach users and what an API endpoint switch costs","description":"## Problem

* We plan to ship a DG MCP server to public users. Some of them are comfortable with git and many are not. We don't yet know how a new server version reaches people who installed it, especially for local (stdio) servers.
* MCP tools will start by calling an internal endpoint (`api/v1/internal/nodes/[nodeId]`). Later they may call an external endpoint (`api/v1/nodes/[nodeId]`) that returns a different output shape. We need to know what that switch costs before we commit to a distribution model.

## Solution

* Survey the ways an MCP server can be distributed: npx/uvx, pinned or unpinned packages, git checkout, Docker, MCP bundles (.mcpb/DXT), registries and directories, and remote HTTP. For each one, record how an update reaches users and who has to act.
* Map the work needed to repoint a tool from the internal to the external endpoint. Cover the server code, tool schemas and descriptions, client caching (`tools/list_changed`), backward compatibility for users who don't update, and auth.

## Done When

* A hand-off doc compares the distribution options by update propagation, user effort, and fit for git-savvy and non-technical public users, and recommends one.
* The doc lists the concrete steps and the rough effort for the internal-to-external endpoint switch under the recommended option, including how users on old versions are handled.

## Out of Scope

* Implementing the distribution pipeline or the external API.
* Choosing the auth design for the external API, beyond noting how it affects the switch.

content.text:
I created the ticket and finished the research. The write-up is a [hand-off doc](https://claude.ai/artifact/6X7VzgFaHLZiJLcsXKTv3B), linked from the ticket. It's private for now, so you'll need to share it from the page's Share menu before Michael can open it.

**Ticket:** [ENG-2512 Research how MCP server updates reach users and what an API endpoint switch costs](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2512/research-how-mcp-server-updates-reach-users-and-what-an-api-endpoint). It's in Ticket Draft, under *Headless DG retrieval API and MCP from database*, labelled Created by Claude and Research, and waiting for your review. Branch: `eng-2512-research-how-mcp-server-updates-reach-users-and`.

**How updates reach users of a local MCP**
- With the spec's `npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest`, a new npm release runs for each user the next time their agent client restarts the MCP. They don't need to run anything. I checked this in the npm source on this machine: `@latest` re-checks the registry on every launch.
- **Nobody is told.** No client shows an update notice for a local MCP, and we have no way to see who is on an old version.
- **We can't hold anyone back.** A breaking release reaches everyone on their next restart.
- **Some users stay on old versions.** People who never restart, who pin a version, or who installed it globally keep running old code.
- **Other options:**
  - A downloadable bundle (`.mcpb`) is easier to install but needs a manual reinstall for every update. The Claude directory has also stopped taking new ones.
  - A git checkout only works for developers.
  - A hosted MCP gives instant updates, but it needs the hosted credential store the 2026-11-10 meeting rejected.

**Cost of switching a tool from `api/v1/internal/nodes/[nodeId]` to `api/v1/nodes/[nodeId]`**
- **The internal route becomes public once a published version calls it.** Old installed copies keep calling it indefinitely, so the additive-only rule applies to it too.
- **Cheapest (a day or two):** change the code behind the route the MCP already calls, and keep returning the old shape. No MCP release.
- **Medium (about a week):** release a new MCP version that calls the new route and converts its response to the old tool output.
- **Most expensive:** expose the new output shape. The shape is enforced, and agents and skills depend on field names, so do this only under a new tool name.
- These effort sizes are my judgement, not measured.

**Recommendation:** keep the local npx `@latest` MCP. Add three things to its first release:
- a version header on every API call;
- an `upgrade_required` error that the agent can pass on to the user;
- a version field in the saved session file.

Each takes about a day, and they're cheapest to add before anyone has installed it. Section 4 of the doc lists the exact edits for `headless-mcp-retrieval`, which is the spec behind your Roam block igzkQFr4r. I haven't touched those files.

Not verified, and listed in the doc's open items:
- how Codex and Claude Desktop cache the tool list;
- what npx does offline;
- how much startup time the registry check adds.

- One retrieval service: every client, the MCP included, goes through the API. - Reuse existing data, vectors, converters and access rules. - The database enforces the agent session's read-only access, not the MCP. - Sync gaps are reported as errors, never as partial content. **Non-Goals:** - A new identity system. - A hosted MCP. - A second embedding pipeline. - Attachment access. - Auditing. ## Decisions ### 1. The API is the retrieval service; the MCP is its client ```mermaid flowchart LR plugin["Roam / Obsidian plugin"] -- "connect command:
bundle with refresh token, shown once" --> connect["mcp connect
(one-time CLI step)"] connect -- "saves the session" --> state[("Local state file")] agent["Agent client
Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex"] -- "stdio" --> mcp["Local MCP"] state --- mcp mcp -- "HTTPS + session token" --> api["Retrieval API
apps/website /api/v1"] api --> fns["Retrieval functions
packages/database"] fns --> db[("Supabase Postgres
row-level security")] api -- "search text only" --> emb["OpenAI embeddings API
turns query text into a vector"] ``` OpenAI here is only the embeddings service that turns a search query into a vector, the same one sync already uses. It isn't ChatGPT, which stays unsupported. ---- ### 3. Hand over a session through `mcp-session-access` `mcp-session-access` (the [session handoff spec](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kPg_0_-lh)) defines the handoff: - **Handoff.** 1. The plugin opens a new session for the space account, using a second client that neither persists nor auto-refreshes. 2. It registers the session with `register_mcp_session(label)`. 3. It shows the bundle once: Supabase URL, anon key, space ID and refresh token. It keeps no copy. - **Registry.** `mcp_session` (list of handed-over sessions) records the session ID (taken from the caller's own token), the label, the space account and the creation time. - **Sign-out.** The holder can sign itself out with local scope (only its own session). Per-session sign-out from the plugin is proposed for right after v0. - **Emergency switch.** Until then, the cut-off is to sign out every other session of the space account. That also signs out the other plugin instances, which sign back in with the space login. - **Who can connect.** Any plugin user of the space. **Tokens.** Two tokens are involved: - the **session token** is the session's short-lived access token, the one the API takes; - the **refresh token** renews the session token, and it rotates on every use. The bundle carries only the refresh token. So the holder's first session token comes from a refresh, and it already carries `mcp_reader` (read-only database role; Decision 4). The plugin discards the `authenticated` session token it used to register. **Alternative (2026-09-25 version):** Option B, a separate agent account for each grant, with a credential issued from a website page. The 2026-11-10 meeting judged its security gain marginal for the extra work. ### 4. The database makes handed-over sessions read-only (A2) Under Option A2 ([decision](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/guIcK3Z9M)), the agent signs in as the space account, but the database makes its session read-only. The session token also works against Supabase directly, outside the API, so the database is what enforces read-only. **The hook.** A custom access token hook (a database function Supabase calls on every token issue and refresh) checks the token's `session_id`. When the session is in `mcp_session` (list of handed-over sessions), it sets the token's `role` claim to `mcp_reader` (read-only database role; name proposed). Other sessions keep `authenticated`. **The role.** `mcp_reader`: - is granted to `authenticator` (the role Supabase's REST layer logs in as), so requests can switch to it; - has `SELECT` on the tables and views retrieval reads, and no `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE`; - has `EXECUTE` only on an allowlist: the search RPC, plus the access helpers that the policies and views call. **Granting functions.** The default privileges don't cover a new role, so `mcp_reader` starts with no `EXECUTE`. It gets an explicit allowlist: the search RPC, plus the existing helpers that the views and policies it reads call, such as `my_space_ids` and `my_accessible_resources`. The allowlist starts from `anon`'s read-only set, which public access already uses. Postgres checks a function called inside a view or policy against the querying role, so a missing grant fails the read with a permission error ([security model](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/blob/main/packages/database/doc/security_model.md), rules 1-2). A new read function that retrieval reaches needs a grant to `mcp_reader` too. Plugin and sync grants don't change. A test lists every function `mcp_reader` can execute and compares the list with the allowlist. Policies without a `TO` clause cover `mcp_reader`, so its reads follow the space account's current access. **Supabase Auth requests aren't covered by the role.** A handed-over session could ask Auth to replace the space login, which would lock out the plugins and let it open sessions that can write. This change turns on the **space login lock** (`secure_password_change` and "require current password"), which refuses that without the current space login. A session could also sign out the plugins' sessions; the plugins just sign back in, and signing out the handed-over session ends it. **A switched-off hook fails open.** Handed-over sessions would then get `authenticated`. The MCP refuses to start unless its session token carries `mcp_reader`, which catches a misconfigured project at setup. **Revocation waits for token expiry.** Sign-out stops refresh, but the current session token stays valid for up to `jwt_expiry` (session token lifetime, 3600 s). The 2026-11-10 meeting accepted this.
